challenges.title: Scale Climber

challenges.title: Stay in Key
challenges.desc: 30 notes, no spicy ones. Improvise freely.

challenges.desc: Watch a melody that grows each round, then play it back.

challenges.desc: How many in-key notes can you fit into 15 seconds?

challenges.desc: A note name appears. Track it down on the keys.

challenges.desc: Leap a 3rd, 5th or octave above the shown note.

challenges.desc: Tap the dot pattern on any key. Gaps matter, notes do not.

challenges.title: Glissando Dash

challenges.title: Daily Challenge

games.title: Zombie Lanes
games.blurb: Zombies march down the lanes toward your keys. Play the note on the zombie to blast it.

games.title: Jiu-Jitsu Flow
games.blurb: Roll on the mats. Answer your partner's moves with the right notes, keep the flow, and earn your belts.

games.title: Runway Remix
games.blurb: Style a model through the eras of music, then play the era's piece on the beat so they strut the runway.

games.title: BachDoom
games.blurb: Clashing-note demons invade the cathedral. Only real music can stop them. Final boss: Bach's Prelude in C.

emulators.title: Theremin
emulators.blurb: Leon Theremin invented an instrument you play without touching it: your hand near one antenna changes the pitch, and your other hand near a second antenna changes the ...

emulators.title: Ondes Martenot
emulators.blurb: Maurice Martenot built this instrument so you could slide your finger on a ring and make a voice-like electronic note.

emulators.title: Tonewheel Organ
emulators.blurb: Laurens Hammond made an organ without pipes: spinning metal wheels made tiny electric hums, and sliding drawbars mixed them together like a recipe.

emulators.title: Tape Keyboard
emulators.blurb: Each key on a Mellotron pressed a strip of recorded tape against a spinning roller, so one keyboard could sound like a whole orchestra.

emulators.title: Voltage-controlled modular / Minimoog-style
emulators.blurb: In 1964 Robert Moog showed that one voltage could steer another: oscillators, a filter and an envelope wired together made an instrument.

emulators.title: ARP 2600-style
emulators.blurb: The 2600 was a "semi-modular" synth: it worked out of the box, but sliders and patch cables let you rewire it, so it was great for learning how sound is built.

emulators.title: TB-303-style bass
emulators.blurb: This little silver box was made to play bass lines for guitarists to practise with, and it flopped.

emulators.title: Programmable polyphonic synth (Prophet-5 spirit)
emulators.blurb: The Prophet-5 was the first synth that could play five notes at once AND remember your sounds with a tiny computer chip.

emulators.title: Chorus polysynth (Juno-style)
emulators.blurb: The Juno was cheap, light and easy: one knob for each job, so you could make a good sound in seconds.

emulators.title: Digital FM synth (DX-style)
emulators.blurb: FM synthesis makes one sound wave wobble the pitch of another, super fast, until it turns glassy, bell-like or bright.
